title: Digital accessibility: why it improves the experience for everyone
description: A moment of frustration trying to cancel an order became the starting point: why accessibility is the foundation of a well-made product, plus a practical checklist for designers and devs.
updateNote: Revised in October 2026: I added what has changed since publication and a new visual to explain the core idea.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: an explorable design system, with tokens, components, contrast and governance.

blocks.text: You know that frustration when you just want to cancel an order on iFood and you simply can't find the button? Yep. That happened to me this week.
I was in a hurry, ordered the wrong thing and thought: “no problem, I'll just cancel it right here.” Except that “right here” wasn't so simple.
I scrolled up, scrolled down, tapped the order icon, went to support, read between the lines… nothing.
In the end, I lost time, got annoyed and couldn't solve my problem.
Now imagine if I had a visual, motor or cognitive disability.
If it was already hard for me with 100% vision, imagine for someone who relies on a screen reader or navigates with only a keyboard?
This kind of situation is more common than it seems, and it shows how a lack of accessibility directly affects the user experience.
Accessibility is about making things easier, not harder
A lot of people still think digital accessibility only serves a “minority.” But check out these numbers:

items: 16% of the world's population lives with some form of disability (WHO, 2023)
More than 2.5 billion people use assistive technologies (UN, 2022)
Only 3% of websites are considered truly accessible (WebAIM, 2023)
In Brazil, more than 45 million people have some degree of disability (IBGE, 2022 Census)
70% of users with disabilities abandon an inaccessible website (Click-Away Pound, 2021)

blocks.text: In other words: accessibility is for everyone. It's not an “extra feature,” it's part of the foundation of a well-made digital product.
Accessibility and user experience go hand in hand
If iFood's cancel order button had been more visible, more intuitive or had a clear visual hierarchy, maybe I wouldn't be here telling this story.

blocks.text: This shows how closely accessibility is tied to usability, and how much good design needs to anticipate different contexts of use, abilities and limitations.

blocks.text: And there's more: it prevents legal problems. In the United States, for example, lawsuits against inaccessible websites passed 4,000 cases a year. In Brazil, the Brazilian Inclusion Law (No. 13,146/2015) already sets mandatory guidelines for digital accessibility.
Practical accessibility checklist for designers and devs
Want to improve the experience for everyone in your product? Here's a simple but powerful checklist:

blocks.caption: Six checklist items that come up most often in interface reviews.

items: Minimum contrast of 4.5:1 between text and background
Font size adjustable through the browser
Large buttons with a comfortable click area
Errors with clear feedback (e.g. “Enter your CPF in the format 000.000.000-00”)
Avoid relying on color alone to convey messages
Links with descriptive labels (e.g. “see product details” instead of “click here”)

blocks.text: Pro tip: validate your layout with tools like WAVE, axe or Figma's built-in features.
Accessibility is design that thinks about everyone
Digital accessibility isn't just a technical requirement. It's an act of empathy. It's thinking about the product as something that should serve all people, not just the majority.
If you're designing interfaces, writing code or planning flows, you have the power to include or exclude people.
And if you've ever been through a frustration like mine with iFood, you know how one poorly made detail can ruin a simple experience.
So, next time you're reviewing a design, ask:
“Can anyone use this comfortably and independently?”
Because accessibility isn't about checking a box. It's about ensuring fairer, more human and more memorable digital experiences.
What has changed since this post
WCAG 2.2, published by the W3C in October 2023, became the current reference. It brought criteria that speak directly to day-to-day product work:

items: Visible focus that doesn't get hidden behind sticky headers or banners.
Minimum touch area of 24 by 24 pixels for interactive targets.
An alternative to drag gestures, with buttons or simple clicks.
Login without depending on memorizing or transcribing codes.

blocks.text: In Europe, the European Accessibility Act took effect in June 2025 for many digital products and services. In Brazil, the Brazilian Inclusion Law already treats accessibility as a right. In other words: it's no longer an extra.

blocks.caption: The same text in different shades. The contrast ratio is calculated on the fly and compared with WCAG thresholds.

blocks.text: Contrast is one of the easiest criteria to check and one of the most forgotten. Light gray on a white background looks elegant in Figma and disappears on a phone screen in the sun.
